name: Median Splits
description: The median of an array $$$b_1, b_2, \ldots b_m$$$, written as $$$\operatorname{med}(b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_m)$$$, is the $$$\left\lceil \frac{m}{2} \right\rceil$$$-th$$$^{\text{∗}}$$$ smallest element of array $$$b$$$. You are given an array of integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ and an integer $$$k$$$. You need to determine whether there exists a pair of indices $$$1 \le l \lt r \lt n$$$ such that: $$$$$$\operatorname{med}(\operatorname{med}(a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_l), \operatorname{med}(a_{l+1}, a_{l+2}, \ldots, a_r), \operatorname{med}(a_{r+1}, a_{r+2}, \ldots, a_n)) \le k.$$$$$$ In other words, determine whether it is possible to split the array into three contiguous subarrays$$$^{\text{†}}$$$ such that the median of the three subarray medians is less than or equal to $$$k$$$. $$$^{\text{∗}}$$$$$$\lceil x \rceil$$$ is the ceiling function which returns the least integer greater than or equal to $$$x$$$. $$$^{\text{†}}$$$An array $$$x$$$ is a subarray of an array $$$y$$$ if $$$x$$$ can be obtained from $$$y$$$ by the deletion of several (possibly, zero or all) elements from the beginning and several (possibly, zero or all) elements from the end.
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \le t \le 10^4$$$). The description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains two integers $$$n$$$ and $$$k$$$ ($$$3 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$, $$$1 \le k \le 10^9$$$) — the length of the array $$$a$$$ and the constant $$$k$$$. The second line of each test case contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$1 \le a_i \le 10^9$$$) — the elements of the array $$$a$$$. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$2 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each testcase, output " YES " if such a split exists, and " NO " otherwise. You can output the answer in any case (upper or lower). For example, the strings " yEs ", " yes ", " Yes ", and " YES " will be recognized as positive responses.

sample_testcases.output:
YES
NO
NO
YES
YES
YES

approach_summary: Verify predicate monotonicity: P(x) is true for x ≤ K and false otherwise. Binary search over the answer domain to find the boundary in O(log(Range) × Verify_Time).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 2103C — Median Splits [33. Binary Search]
topic_editorial.summary: Binary search on the monotonic answer domain.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The predicate function $P(x)$ ('Is answer $\le x$ feasible?') is monotonic: if $P(x)$ is true for some value, it remains true for all larger values (or vice versa). This allows binary division of the answer search space $[\text{low}, \text{high}]$ in $O(\log(\text{Range}))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N \log(\text{Range}))$
  The binary search divides the search interval by 2 at each iteration, requiring $\log_2(\text{Range})$ steps. In each step, the feasibility check `check(mid)` scans the array in $\mathcal{O}(N)$ time.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(1)$ auxiliary space
  The algorithm operates directly over the input array without allocating extra auxiliary memory.
